The Courtyard Marriott was bustling that weekend. In addition to being the go-to hotel for the conference, it was also hosting a meeting for the California Statewide Law Enforcement Association. Just down the street, at the Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk, there was a marching band competition.

I felt confident in my ability to sort the crowd into their respective categories—band nerd, monster nerd, cop. So I said to the man waiting for the elevator wearing a hoodie with a colorful demon embossed on the front: You must be here for the monster conference. His eyes widened: You mean real monsters? Having a conference? He looked genuinely concerned. No, I assured him. Academics. People who read monster stories and talk about them. He seemed relieved and told me he was just visiting because he thought Santa Cruz was “dope.”

Santa Cruz is a fitting place for a monster conference. Besides historically being a sanctuary for weirdos and misfits, it has served as a backdrop for a bevy of horror classics, including The Lost Boys, Killer Klowns from Outer Space, and Jordan Peele’s Us. The mascot for UC Santa Cruz is a banana slug, which, while not technically a monster, does show the college’s affinity for the slimy and betentacled.

The group of monster experts waiting for the shuttle to the opening reception, at the Santa Cruz Museum of Art and History, looked tamer than I expected, sensibly dressed and well-coiffed. When I told them I was a journalist, I got a chilly reception. In the van someone explained to me that the conference organizers had sent out a warning about a right-wing journalist who was working on a hit piece about the event. While monster studies had gradually become accepted inside the academy, it also seemed to epitomize tendencies that have been ridiculed by conservatives. More than three years ago, when Florida governor Ron DeSantis laid out his plans to overhaul higher education by mandating an emphasis on Western civilization and eliminating diversity programs, he said: “We don’t want students to go through, at taxpayer expense, and graduate with a degree in zombie studies.”

The conference attendees had, broadly, two theories about why they were being targeted by the right. The first was that the field was seen as impractical: How does studying the history of Godzilla make students productive, tax-paying members of society? The second was about monster studies’ entanglement with queer studies, disability studies, feminism, and critical race theory. Monsters are often metaphors for people on society’s edges—the word monstre was even used in the fourteenth century to refer to people and animals born with abnormalities or disabilities. Studying the meaning and history of monsters is inherently an exploration of diversity.

In other words, some think monster studies is under attack because it is perceived as useless, while others think it is under attack because of what it is useful for. In this respect the response to the field reflected the larger war on the humanities, as departments across the country were targeted for being both too “woke” and too useless in the job market.

The opening reception was small, with finger food and nonalcoholic drinks. Wandering around the crowd, I met a young academic and writer balancing a paper plate of appetizers in her hand. She told me she studied cryptids like Bigfoot and explained her anthropological interests in how people construct narratives. It was fascinating work, but I hadn’t been able to stop thinking about what Chemers had told me about the monster as a portal for personal discovery. I asked if studying monsters had transformed her. “Absolutely,” she said, and pointed to her name tag, which identified her pronouns as “she” and “it.” She explained that she was neurodivergent and queer. “I’ve had these moments of feeling like I was inhuman,” she said. But monster studies had taught her that she didn’t need to be palatable or normative to exist. She embraced herself as a monster: “It pronouns have brought me a lot of joy.”

We took our seats for the first keynote of the weekend, by David Livingstone Smith, a professor of philosophy at the University of New England, who was presenting his book Making Monsters: The Uncanny Power of Dehumanization. He flicked through slides showing how marginalized groups have been depicted as monsters by those in power: Jewish people drawn as humanoid rats in Nazi Germany; a newspaper clipping from North Carolina in 1898 showing a Black man with bat wings and claws, standing on a ballot box.

Then he paused and told us the next slides were ones he’d been increasingly forced to censor when presenting on college campuses. First, a picture of Donald Trump with his infamous quote, “Democrats say, ‘Please don’t call [immigrants] animals, they’re humans. I said, ‘No, they’re not humans, they’re animals.’” And then former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant saying, “We are fighting human animals and we are acting accordingly.”

Advertisement

This wasn’t a trend you needed a scholar to point out. But Livingstone Smith had a somewhat subtler observation to make. Racist and antisemitic propaganda doesn’t show just rats and bats—they have human faces. The imagined beasts are hybrids, impossibilities, creatures that don’t follow rules or fit into categories. He listed creatures that were frightening, but not monsters: grizzly bears, mosquitoes carrying West Nile virus. “These are all physically threatening beings. We need something else to make them monsters,” he explained. A monster must be uncanny—creepy and unsettling; it must disrupt our sense of reality, must be, to use Livingstone Smith’s term, “metaphysically threatening.” Zombies are both dead and alive. Werewolves are man and beast. This is how monsterization of people works too: Jewish people, in Nazi propaganda, were both weak and able to control the entire world.

The morning after the opening reception, I caught the shuttle from the hotel to the UC Santa Cruz campus. We passed a group of preteens on bikes, and at the very back was a kid who looked to be six or seven years old, peddling furiously to keep up with the older crowd. He was wearing a helmet with rubber spikes protruding from the top, making him appear like a miniature Godzilla. Someone in the van pointed: Look at that! That’s a little monster. That’s our guy! Everyone cheered. Go little monster! Go!

The conference panels covered a wide range of topics, from medieval artifacts to the Tyler Perry TV show Beauty in Black. The theme for the year, loosely followed, was “nourishment,” so panels sometimes focused on food. There was, just before lunch, a presentation called “Snacking in Hell.” The audience squirmed in their chairs at the descriptions of eating in Dante’s Inferno: a man chewing another man where his neck joins his brain, like a hunk of bread. Then everyone went off to eat a conference lunch of warmed-over chicken and pita.

Many of the sessions considered monsters to be sympathetic, if complicated, creatures. The hydra, the multiheaded monster from Greek myth, was presented as a powerful symbol of collective action. A panel on “freakery” argued that the disabled people featured in circus and carnival freak shows could be viewed as prodigious monsters: not less than human but stretching the boundaries of what people could be. The panelists largely seemed to see monsters as oracles that reveal some essential truth or heroes that show us the way to be better humans. Go little monsters! Go!

Leaving one of these sessions, I found Livingstone Smith sitting at a picnic table outside, looking somber and a bit out of place. He squinted under the bright sun. This conference was his first foray into what he called the “monstersphere.” Usually he attended conferences with other philosophers, where he dissected some of the most violent chapters of human history. He was a bit baffled by the apparent adoration of monsters that he witnessed here. To him, monsters were made to justify atrocities; to view them with such reverence stretched the definition of the word. Looking at the crowd milling around us, I felt a kind of whiplash: a person wearing silver skeleton hands pinned to their shirt, a scholar wearing a Creepshow T-shirt, two teachers handing out miniature rubber ducks in monster costumes—Frankenstein’s monster, Dracula, a ghost.

At the second keynote speech, Kimberly J. Lau, a professor of literature at UC Santa Cruz, asked a question that could be provocative to a room full of monster-lovers: What does it mean for the monster to stop being scary? These days, she said, “monsters are everywhere around us, and they’re definitely the cool kids. Edgy, hip, darkly attractive, we want to be near them, want to be them.” While she spoke, she showed slides of the Wicked Witch of the West (now the hero of the musical Wicked) and Sleeping Beauty’s Maleficent (given a sympathetic treatment in her eponymous 2014 movie). What do we lose when we no longer have monsters to describe things that are legitimately terrifying? “We need to have a language for that,” Lau told me later. “It feels dangerous for all our monsters to be so sympathetic.”

Were monsters a useful metaphor to wrestle with evil? Did we need the word for people who committed genuinely horrific acts: rape, genocide, torture? Lau’s subject was the rise of the so-called “manosphere,” the on- and offline culture that preaches sexual control and celebrates violence against women; she concluded after months of studying everyone from Andrew Tate to Elliott Rodger that maybe it wasn’t monsters she was interested in after all. What she wanted to understand was how cultures like the manosphere are so effective at creating fear by turning other people (women, queer people, or immigrants, say) into monsters. She wanted to look at the monstrosity of the monster makers. After all, the villain is Victor Frankenstein.

The next morning, waiting for the shuttle, I found myself chatting with an Irish academic in a black corset who studies satanism and was “breaking into ghosts.” Another person wore a goblin T-shirt, and when someone complimented them, they said, “I’m just so glad to wear it somewhere that people get the joke.” Everyone laughed and I forced out a giggle, though I had no idea what the joke was.

A few hours later, Jeffrey Jerorme Cohen himself gave the conference’s third and final keynote, “Monster Theory at 30.” Throughout the conference, I’d seen groups of people fall into a nervous hush when he approached. Like a celebrity, he autographed books and posed for selfies.

Chemers, the director of the Santa Cruz monster studies program who had invited me to the conference, introduced Cohen to the eager audience as the “progenitor of our field,” and the audience erupted in applause. Cohen told the crowd he wanted to talk about the monster as an invitation to think through potential. He asked, “How many people…feel like monsters have opened possibilities for them that might not otherwise have been there?” Hands shot up across the room.

Cohen did not paint a tidy picture of monsters that are simply beloved—they can be frightening, and he warned that we’d be fools to downplay their danger. When you talk about monsters as symbols of new possibilities, that includes the possibility of a more terrible and terrifying world. But monsters can also be affirmative by expanding what we think can be real and therefore what we think we can do or become. They should be impossible—the giants that defy the laws of nature, the aliens that resist scientific explanation, the ghosts that rebuke death. “Can we be forgiven for loving the monster when it arrives as messenger, declaring that our categories were always too narrow?” Cohen asked.

We live in precarious times. Fascism is a threat at home and across the globe, and Cohen had noticed a trend of people calling the leaders of these movements monsters. But he argued that using the word to describe them limited the “eloquent potency and enigmatic possibilities of the monster.” He finds these oligarchs and fascists frightening and dangerous, but not philosophically challenging. To him, they were the most predictable and tiresome version of what it means to be human, “more tedious than monstrous, more banal than category-challenging.” “To label them monsters is an insult to monsters,” Cohen said.

On the last night of the conference, after all the sessions were over, there was a “monster’s ball.” Everyone was invited to don a costume and dance. The building had floor-to-ceiling windows, and the light inside reflected off the red walls, giving the whole structure a crimson glow. What looked sterile and academic in the daylight took on an otherworldly splendor. Music pulsed from inside the large room, where just hours before people had delivered lectures. The podium was now covered in purple Christmas lights and pictures of glowing skulls. A bland houseplant next to the podium seemed transformed into wild flora plucked from a jungle.

I asked a man with a black hoodie pulled over his head and his hands shoved in his pockets about his costume. He shook his head no, and put a finger up to his lips, shh. Later he ran by me and cackled into my ear. I laughed and felt afraid at the same time.

I spotted a professor who’d flown from Delhi, India, to present on monsters in children’s literature. She was dressed as a vampire, her long black hair tumbling below her knees. She said the costume made her feel amazing. Her husband chimed in: “It allows her to literally put her hair down. As an academic she’s always so bunched up.” They danced, her hair swaying. Another woman was dressed as Medusa. She chose the costume, she said, because she admires Medusa, who in some versions of the myth is a powerful survivor of sexual assault. Her face glistened with sparkling green paint.

A red-headed woman wearing rose-colored glasses and black antennae told me she was dressed as a mothman, a cryptid that looks like a tall human, but with red eyes and black wings. It’s known to appear just before great tragedies occur. She explained that she loves the ambiguity of the mothman. Does he cause tragedies? Or is he a harbinger, trying to warn people? I asked her how it felt to dress as that monster. She pulled back her shoulders, showing off her black cape, and told me she felt beautiful.

entries.content:
This fall a literary scandal has erupted in France around a debut novel with a dramatic title—C’était ça ou mourir (“It Was Either That or Die”)—by the Haitian-Québécois author Thélyson Orélien. Orélien’s account of a Haitian migrant’s odyssey across South and North America made it onto the best-seller list and secured nominations for all the country’s major literary awards; it was set to be translated into over twenty languages. On September 21 the novel won the Prix du Roman Fnac, an award given by France’s largest book retailer.

That same day a Twitter account called Balance ton Claude (Out your Claude) made a startling accusation. The account’s owners had run many sections of the book through the AI-detection program Pangram, they claimed, which showed widespread use of AI throughout the text. In a country where literature is still treated as a matter of national importance, the allegation got wall-to-wall media coverage and set off an acrimonious, highly politicized controversy. The prestigious Goncourt prize announced that the book had been withdrawn from consideration. Online, right-wing accounts targeted Orélien with racist invective. The Quebec newspaper La Presse reviewed some of Orélien’s older work and said it found several instances of plagiarism in columns and a short story he wrote over a decade ago. The author withdrew from public view; his publishers in Canada and France stood by him and said he was preparing evidence of his innocence.

On October 13 Orélien broke his silence with a statement in which he rejected the accusation against him as “a calumny and a heresy.” He apologized for his earlier plagiarisms, which he called “youthful mistakes,” and acknowledged that he had used AI to do research for his book. But he maintained he had used it for nothing more; he said he wrote the first draft of his novel back in 2017, and that it contained stories he had lived or heard. The book came from his guts, he wrote, and “to credit a machine for writing this text that is mine, that is of my people, is to contest not just my identity as a writer but my humanity.” On October 21 Orélien’s Canadian publisher announced that, based on the results of their own investigation, they were ending their relationship with him.

Balance ton Claude is an anonymous collective originally formed to criticize the AI-generated social media posts of politicians and business leaders. Two of the young men behind the account have come forward: Pierre-Thomas Eckert, a researcher in moral philosophy, and Samuel Fitoussi, a business manager at a venture capital company and a writer and commentator for the right-wing paper Le Figaro, where he has criticized the excesses of “wokisme.” In an editorial in Le Monde they warned of the “existential danger” that AI poses to literature, research, and human intellectual production; their goal, they claimed, was to protect the trust between writers and readers. Yet anonymously lobbing accusations online was hardly the best way to achieve such aims. In fact the Orélien debacle has exposed many currents of suspicion, mistrust, and confusion that flow through the world of French letters; more interestingly, it has opened a debate about what constitutes authorship and how literary merit is measured in the first place.

To many watching the scandal unfold, there was something suspect about the very speed and unseemly glee with which C’était ça ou mourir was denounced across right-wing accounts. “Any accusation against any one of us [writers] will be taken up immediately like a sure thing,” said the writer Virginie Despentes on a TV talk show a few days into the scandal. “As long as it comes from the far right, let’s go, it must be true!” To Orélien’s defenders, the targeting of a Black writer whose book is a sympathetic account of a migrant’s journey to safety was clearly racially and politically motivated. Why, they have asked, was this particular book analyzed? And how reliable is AI-detection software to begin with?

“Orélien does not need to justify himself,” Despentes said. “He can write as he chooses.” Many writers, she went on, “are going to use AI because AI has forced its way into our life,” integrated into word-processing applications and Internet searches. Despentes herself writes by hand in notebooks now, she added, to avoid being given constant AI-generated prompts and suggestions; her own books have been used to train LLMs. “Now I should justify myself, when AI has taken everything without my consent, without asking my opinion…. Fuck Pangram!”

In their editorial, Fitoussi and Eckert insisted that they shared their doubts about Orélien’s novel “without giving a moment’s thought to the novel’s theme, the author’s supposed opinions, and even less—it’s maddening to have to say so—to the color of his skin.” In a subsequent post on Twitter, they even wrote that people should “go easy” on Orélien and that the best thing would be for him to “get back to writing!” This show of sympathy seems highly disingenuous—they must have measured the gravity of their allegation for the writer’s career and anticipated the kind of media firestorm that would engulf him.

Advertisement

Meanwhile the debate has expanded beyond Orélien’s specific case to the future of literature in a world where editors, publishers, and readers can no longer be certain that a book is the product of a particular human consciousness. The general consensus seems to be that the literary establishment is woefully unprepared to deal with a challenge they should have seen coming. Commentators have suggested using AI-detection software as a matter of course or clearly labeling books as composed by a human or an LLM. To do the latter, the philosopher Monique Canto-Sperber wrote in Le Monde, is what honesty—and the survival of publishing—demands: “In a world in which fakes and imitations are spreading, the link between the author and his reader remains one of the rare relationships of sincerity and trust.” (EU legislation that should come into effect next year mandates that AI-generated text, audio, and video contain digital markers that will make it easier to detect.)

Others are taking a longer historical view. In an interview with the radio program France Culture, the literature professor William Marx, whose books include Adieu to Literature: History of a Devaluation (2005), noted that it has only been “since the eighteenth century that the idea of the author, tied to that of originality, has crystallized.” Nineteenth-century novelists like Alexandre Dumas still had workshops of writers assisting in their prodigious production. These early ghostwriters were called prête-plumes or, wincingly, nègres—a term that makes clear the assumed hierarchy in the ability to create, the very hierarchy that a Black writer’s commercial and critical success would upset.

Marx wondered whether we may be reaching the end of a “democratic parenthesis of literature,” an era of mass reading and writing. He envisaged a future in which the greater part of literature could be written and read by machines and only a small community would still read and write in the laborious old ways, keeping alive an art form that balances the need for expressivity and sincerity—for “the illusion of access to another soul”—and the need for formal efficacy, a full mastery of narrative and linguistic tools. Marx seems to expect, as do quite a few others, that AI will be able to master those tools fully at some point in the near future. Yet even if that did happen, readers might well continue to insist on having the first need met as well. For all the spread and popularity of AI-generated content, there remains a countervailing demand for authenticity. Part of the appeal of C’était ça ou mourir, after all, was the promise of a unique voice, grounded in the author’s own life, that could directly convey the dramatic and painful experience of migration.

Throughout the controversy, Orélien’s book has continued to sell. In late September I bought it in a bookshop in Montpellier, where it was prominently displayed with a glowing, handwritten recommendation note by the staff. Perhaps readers don’t care as much as is supposed about the use of AI; perhaps they don’t trust AI detectors any more than literary critics to tell them what is worth reading; perhaps they are simply curious.

I read the book myself with some of that same curiosity. I could not say if it was written with AI assistance; it does have many repetitions and many of those supposedly telltale sets of three. Mostly I was struck by other shortcomings.

The narrator is a Haitian history-geography professor named Jonas who on the opening pages sees his home go up in flames and his neighborhood invaded by militias. (We learn very little of the political or economic situation in Haiti—only that “the country was dead. It wasn’t a country anymore, just a pretext. A sign. A torn banknote.”) He packs a pair of underwear, a photograph of his mother, and a book of poems into a knapsack and spends the rest of the book on the move.

He also spends it describing everything he sees and experiences in highly metaphorical, lyrical terms. Here is how he presents the batey, a settlement built around a sugarcane factory:

A batey is a country within the country. A sugarcane shantytown that shelters those who have no papers and are ready to work for next to nothing—ghosts you can buy on credit. The wooden shacks line up like excuses, the tin roofs sing at the slightest rain, the dogs sleep on shoes to stay warm. Children play with bits of wood, women sell no-good doughnuts, men call each other “boss” to remember they were free once upon a time. The batey has a smell: molasses and fatigue. In it one hears the sound, day and night, of metal rubbing against resignation.

Overall, the world of the book lacks edges; it is blanketed in a soft layer of banal and sometimes nonsensical poeticization. The narrator laughs often, yet the way his laughter is described (“A dry, thin laugh, twisted like a tree that grew in a street with no sunshine”) rarely conjured any form of real laughter for me, just as I could hardly picture the neighborhood he left behind—“a giant ashtray, a cemetery without tombs, a theater of the absurd where the roles changed with every burst of gunfire.” People’s behavior is equally hard to parse. On his way out of his neighborhood Jonas sits down on the side of the road, pulls out his notebook, and writes, “Today, I lost my house, but I found my escape.” He crosses paths with a woman with two children leashed to her with a rope. She tells him: “This way, if one dies, I won’t have to look for the other.” I find it hard to imagine any mother speaking of her children this way.

Advertisement

Everyone the narrator meets gets one or two lines of this kind. When he arrives at an aunt’s house in the Dominican Republic, she asks not what happened or how long he plans to stay with her, but: “Jonas, do you think you will be able to spend your life running away?” A border guard tells him: “You have too much truth in your gaze.” On the road he tastes “the flavor of days that pass by without recognizing you”—while I couldn’t help wondering what he was actually eating, day after unemployed and wandering day. Perhaps he is meant to be a dreamy troubadour, an unreal stand-in for all those who are in search of a new home. Yet every chapter ends with the same emotional beat: poetic resignation, self-deprecating but heroic determination.

If Orélien’s editors and publishers should be taken to task, it is less for not suspecting the use of AI than for being blinded by the marketability of the author’s biography, identity, and subject matter and for trumpeting as groundbreaking a book that is quite sentimental and safe, that does little to trouble its readers’ expectations. There is nothing new in a middling book finding huge success. But the fact that so many people professed to love and be moved by a novel that may have been written with AI (to what degree and in what manner, we will likely never know) raises a troubling question: Is there anything particular, inimitable, about human intelligence and expressivity? As the French science fiction writer Alain Damasio has suggested, AI’s ability to make us doubt this is the “ultimate narcissistic wound.”

Right-wing commentators in France have had a field day compiling the exaggerated praise that the literary establishment showered on Orélien. To them it is evident that the “the left” championed him for ideological rather than literary reasons. But their own satisfaction in exposing the author and embarrassing the literary elite is also nakedly political; it has nothing to do with caring about literature. This is a sad debacle in which almost everyone has lost out, no one more than the writer himself. He is of course responsible for his own choices, but one cannot but feel sorry for Orélien. His overhyped success, glaring media exposure, and sudden fall from grace—it has all been a vertiginous process in which he has been tokenized and essentialized, made a stand-in and symbol, from all sides. He now faces the devastating brunt of an online pile-on and a national controversy.

One of the most lucid, elegant, and even-handed analyses of the debate around Orélien’s book was a Facebook post by the Senegalese writer Mohamed Mbougr Sarr, who won the Goncourt in 2021 for a marvelous novel, The Most Secret History of Men, partly inspired by an earlier literary scandal with striking parallels to the one around C’était ça ou mourir. In 1968 the Malian writer Yambo Ouologuem won a major French literary award for his novel Le devoir de violence. Accused of plagiarizing passages in the book, he said they were intended to be clear citations and had originally been in quotation marks. The scandal ended his literary career; he retired into the countryside in Mali and into silence. In his novel, Sarr imagined his own version of a Ouologuem-like figure and sent a young African writer on an obsessive search for his cursed literary forefather.

“None of what is happening is completely new,” Sarr writes in his post. “We could almost say that we are within a tradition: that of an easy doubt, or rather, a doubt that takes easily when the writer who is its object is Black.” There is nothing inherently racist about expressing concern over a Black author’s plagiarism or alleged use of AI, Sarr notes, but one cannot “minimize the racial dimensions of the accusations”—the manner in which they were made, amplified, and received.

They also seem to be part of a pattern: again and again these controversies feature authors of color. Last year in the UK Jason Arday, the youngest Black professor ever hired at Cambridge, was accused of plagiarism by another scholar who had expressed openly racist views. Cambridge opened an investigation into his work and hiring, and the British press hounded him relentlessly; Arday resigned and soon after killed himself. In the past year accusations of using LLMs have been leveled against the Caribbean writer Jamir Nazir, whose story “The Serpent in the Grove” won the Commonwealth Prize in the UK, and Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza, the Zimbabwean winner of the Caine Prize for African Writing. (Both Nazir and Kundizeza denied the allegations.) In most of these cases, the accusers have used Pangram or other AI-detection software to bolster their claims. As Sarr observes, there is a long history of such charges creating a much greater uproar when they are aimed at Black writers than at their peers, who may face similar accusations without experiencing the same consequences. “It even happens that despite confirmed plagiarism, uncredited borrowings, these authors continue to publish and to win prizes, including the most prestigious ones.”

Sarr hasn’t been the only one to point out double standards. When I discussed this article with French friends, several immediately mentioned the Algerian writer Kamel Daoud, who won the Goncourt in 2024 for his novel Houris. The protagonist of that book is a woman who has forever lost the ability to speak. When she was a child, Islamist militias fighting in the Algerian Civil War massacred her family and slit her throat, leaving her to breathe for the rest of her life through a cannula inserted in her windpipe. An Algerian woman named Saâda Arbane, who survived a similar massacre and suffers from the same condition, was a patient of Daoud’s psychiatrist wife. Arbane has sued the author in Algeria and France, claiming that he stole details of her life as well as confidential information she shared in her therapy sessions. She says that Daoud approached her about writing a book about her and that, after she declined his request, he went ahead anyway.

Daoud defended himself by casting Arbane’s allegations as a plot by the Algerian government—which he has often criticized, and which censors discussions of the civil war—to harass and silence him; the French media and literary establishment largely adopted this view and closed ranks around him in the name of supporting freedom of speech. By positioning his work first and foremost within a clash-of-civilizations discourse in France (where Daoud lives and often writes as a critical voice on Islam and Arab societies generally), he was able to almost entirely sidestep the question of whether he had committed a grave ethical violation.

There is no easy way out of deciding what a book means to us, whether it enchants us enough to make us believe in it; or of deciding who a story originally belongs to, and how much that matters. The advent of AI has exacerbated these anxieties. Sarr and others are rightly skeptical of the idea that submitting writing to AI-detection software is the way to ensure fairness or trust. To rely on such software, he wrote in his post, is to continue to nourish AI, to make it “not just a referee but a god who will decide what is human and not-human,” and to “forget that racist, condescending biases exist within the AI systems’ ways of reading and evaluating. It’s a bad idea and a huge loss of time; but above all it’s a significant loss of intellectual, political, moral autonomy,” Sarr wrote. “I read here and there that we are entering a new era of suspicion. If that is true, we are the ones creating it.”

entries.title: Picture This
entries.summary: Throughout the history of print, illustrators have helped visualize writer’s stories, and at times became storytellers themselves.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Henry James loved pictures, but not when they threatened to supplement his words. For James, “responsible prose” should be “pictorial enough, above all in itself”—the phrase comes from his preface to The Golden Bowl (1909)—and anything that offered to relieve it of that responsibility risked short-circuiting the process by which good writers should stimulate the imaginative capacity of their readers. “As regards illustrations you will of course please yourself,” he observed resignedly to the editor of The Century Magazine, Robert Underwood Johnson, in 1887. “I frankly confess that I hate them when attached to my own prose—& like them only as an incident of that of others.”

James lost that particular battle when The Century published the travel essay in question, “London,” with thirteen illustrations by the American artist Joseph Pennell the following year. But with the partial exception of the frontispieces that Scribner’s commissioned from the photographer Alvin Langdon Coburn for the so-called New York Edition of 1907–1909, James mostly succeeded in keeping his novels and tales free of illustration. Writing about visual art was one thing—the narrator of a story also submitted to The Century in 1887 happens to be a portrait painter—but James preferred that the magazine print “The Liar” “pictureless,” as he put it with characteristic emphasis to Johnson. “Ah, your illustrations—your illustrations,” he exclaimed wryly, “how, as a writer, one hates ’em; & how their being as good as they are makes one hate ’em more!”

James’s resistance to illustration doesn’t figure in D.B. Dowd’s new history of the practice, Reading Pictures, though the writer who liked such images well enough when they accompanied the work of others does make two brief appearances, both quotations from his 1893 collection of essays on the subject, Picture and Text. Though the evidence Dowd has assembled suggests that James was clearly exaggerating when he announced at the outset that “the illustration of books, and even more of magazines, may be said to have been born in our time,” the novelist wasn’t wrong to think that he lived in a century when words and images could be combined in increasingly profitable ways and that publishers were eager to take advantage of the opportunity.

According to the Oxford English Dictionary, it was also in the nineteenth century that the word “illustration”—which originally meant “spiritual enlightenment” or “illumination”—took on the modern sense of a pictorial representation. One of the dictionary’s earliest examples of this new usage, dated 1817, would have resonated with James, since it refers to the engravings after Richard Westall that served as frontispieces for the collected works of Sir Walter Scott, a publishing milestone that in turn provided a principal model for James’s New York Edition and its very different frontispieces almost a hundred years later. It was in James’s time, too, that the professional illustrator was first named as such, at least in English, which Dowd dates to the middle of the century.

Dowd’s book ranges chronologically from the ninth century to the present and geographically from East Asia to America; its more than four hundred images include everything from Buddhist scrolls and illuminated manuscripts to advertising calendars, album covers, and comic strips. Despite its subtitle, this history of illustration isn’t so much a sequential narrative as a series of loosely arranged mini-histories and thematic excurses, some more sharply focused than others. But central to Reading Pictures, both literally and figuratively, is what Dowd calls “the high season of illustrated mass publishing,” which began in the late nineteenth century and continued well into the twentieth. “Illustrations,” he begins by stipulating, are “printed, by definition,” and though a few of the images in his study appear to violate that rule—an oil painting of a fight scene by George Bellows from 1909, for instance, or a drawing by Molly Crabapple of construction workers in Gaza that was apparently published online in 2015—the vast majority of the illustrations in Reading Pictures were first disseminated in print.

What that meant, however, differed markedly over time and from one culture to another. Dowd’s earliest example is dated 868 CE and comes from a seventeen-foot-long Buddhist scroll whose elegant ideographs, like its images, were printed from fixed wooden blocks rather than the movable type that European broadsides and books typically began to combine with woodcuts in the aftermath of Gutenberg’s invention nearly six centuries later. (Such single-block printing is known as xylography, from the Greek xylon, meaning wood or timber.) Though the Gutenberg Bible was not illustrated, a German publisher quickly took advantage of the new technology to issue a book entitled Der Edelstein (The Gemstone, 1461), in which illustrated fables from classical sources were retold in the vernacular by a Dominican monk named Ulrich Boner. As if to advertise the possibilities of the new medium, the monk’s woodcut figure appeared at the beginning of each fable, helpfully pointing to the accompanying image.

Advertisement

Around the same time, European printmakers also began to exploit the potential of copper engraving, a practice that seems to have originated with an anonymous artist known as the Master of the Playing Cards before largely migrating to the reproduction of paintings and sculptures in the seventeenth century. Though the use of chemicals rather than a burin to cut through the plate made the process of etching comparatively faster and more fluid, both of these so-called intaglio methods were more laborious than woodcutting, and both produced prints that had to be tipped or bound into letterpress books, since neither could be simultaneously employed with movable type. Eighteenth-century publishers might supplement their editions of poets and dramatists with engraved illustrations, but such volumes typically remained luxury items. The development of white-line engraving, a technique first perfected by the British artist Thomas Bewick, eventually helped to bring down costs by allowing engravers to incise refined marks directly into durable wooden blocks that could then be used for relief printing.

Bewick is probably most familiar to modern readers as the artist whose depictions of birds and their far-flung origins so fascinate the young heroine in the opening paragraphs of Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre (1847). But his technique really came into its own a few years before the novel was published, when an enterprising editor named Herbert Ingram launched The Illustrated London News (1842), a weekly broadside whose combination of pictures and text—thirty-two wood engravings in each sixteen-page issue—proved especially popular for war reporting. Within a year of its founding, there were French and German equivalents, both also with versions of the word “illustrated” in their titles, and they were followed in the next decade by Frank Leslie’s Illustrated Newspaper (1855) and Harper’s Weekly (1857), among others, in the US.

Like the Crimean War, the American Civil War afforded ample opportunities for the men known as “special artists” to ply their trade, transmitting images directly from the battlefield to their subscribers—or more precisely to the engravers who helped translate their drawings and watercolors into print. (Illustration, as Dowd emphasizes, is a “team sport.”) Though we might imagine that such work was soon overtaken by the camera, that does not appear to have been the case: readers seem to have grown accustomed to the clarity and interpretive power of engraved images, and “for decades after it was possible to print halftone photographs in newspapers,” Dowd reports, “editors declined to do so.”

Indeed, one of the reasons Dowd’s history can sometimes be hard to follow is the unevenness of the phenomena he analyzes. While the visual culture on which he focuses clearly depended on technological changes, these didn’t necessarily succeed one another in chronological order, nor did they migrate consistently from place to place. Even in the West, xylographic books didn’t die out with Gutenberg, as the multiplying word bubbles in two scenes from Life and Acts of St. John the Evangelist (circa 1465–1470) richly demonstrate, while Japanese publishers soon abandoned the movable type imported by the Jesuits in the late sixteenth century and reverted to the use of single blocks that printed calligraphic marks and images simultaneously. In China, too, single-block printing didn’t give way until the introduction of modern lithography in the 1870s, and despite the widespread use of wood engraving in Europe and North America, the Chinese skipped that stage altogether. In both countries the preference for the single block was as much aesthetic as practical: the reflection of a culture in which the appearance of the writing constituted part of the image, and readers had learned to look at the words as well as through them.

Printed images travel easily, however, even if texts await translation. The impact of Japanese prints on nineteenth-century Europe is an old story, but Dowd’s juxtaposition of a poster that Pierre Bonnard designed to advertise Debray’s champagne in 1891 with a ukiyo-e print of a Kabuki actor that Toyohara Kunichika created twenty-five years earlier provides an eye-catching reminder of just how much Western artists learned from their Eastern counterparts. The large black characters of “France-Champagne” that curve boldly across the top of the poster might almost be said to speak Japanese, as they echo the calligraphic outlines of the curly-headed woman and the champagne bubbles that spill from her glass. At virtually the same time, an elaborate print from 1894 celebrating Japan’s victory in the first land battle of the Sino-Japanese War suggests that Western style was also leaving its mark on the East, as several journalists wearing European dress cluster in one corner, two of them busily recording the action live on their drawing boards. Meanwhile the creator of the print, Mizuno Toshikata, apparently remained in Tokyo, working the whole thing up from published accounts, photographs, and his own imagination.

Advertisement

East Asian cartooning, too, absorbed Western influences, from the variations on the satirical weekly Punch that nineteenth-century British expats launched in Japan and briefly in China to the syndicated cartoons from the US that poured into Japan in the 1920s and 1930s. We’ve grown accustomed to thinking of Japanese manga as a booming import—according to Wikipedia, it has been “massively outselling” American comics since the late 2010s—but Reading Pictures suggests that the influence has gone both ways, as modern versions of an older Japanese tradition of graphic narrative were catalyzed by the translated reprints of American strips that readers began to consume almost a hundred years earlier.

An evocative juxtaposition of a 1931 travel poster inviting tourists to explore the romance and beauty of French Indochina with a Vietnamese propaganda poster produced thirty-five years later suggests how tangled these lines of visual transmission could become, as the Japanese-inflected style of Bonnard and others made its way into the curriculum of the colonial art school in Hanoi, where the designer of the travel poster, Jos-Henri Ponchin, taught Đường Ngọc Cảnh, the Vietnamese artist whose arresting image of a young girl with a lotus and an M16 exhorted her compatriots to “Look after the Land, Look after the Youth.” The young woman in Ponchin’s travel poster holds an umbrella rather than an M16, and she carries it at a slightly more relaxed angle than does her counterpart, but the echoes of color and pattern between the two images are nonetheless striking.

Such cross-cultural comparisons are among the rewards of Reading Pictures, even if they threaten to compound the rather dizzying effect of the whole, with its profusion of images and multiplying narratives. No history, of course, really has a singular origin, but Dowd can’t quite seem to decide which of his many chronologies he wishes to highlight. After an initial survey of early modern printing and publishing, he opens his chapter on the visualization of literature with a familiar episode in the history of the British novel: the serendipitous sequence of events by which Charles Dickens came to write The Pickwick Papers (1836–1837) and stumbled on the formula for illustrated fiction that he and his publishers continued to exploit for the rest of his career.

The story, in more than one sense, began when Dickens was invited to compose the text for a series of sporting prints by the caricaturist Robert Seymour, to be issued monthly on the model of Pierce Egan’s best-selling Life in London (1821), a picaresque narrative that had been printed alongside engravings by George and Robert Cruikshank. Dickens was then a little-known journalist and parliamentary reporter—not yet one to class himself among the “important novelists,” as Dowd seems to think—and the assignment was basically hackwork. Seymour took for granted that his was the principal responsibility in the enterprise, but the new recruit had other ideas, and by the second issue he was requesting significant alterations to one of the artist’s designs. Already at risk of bankruptcy and now facing this additional threat to his autonomy, Seymour redrew the plate in question and promptly shot himself through the heart.

The result was not only that Hablot Knight Browne (better known as “Phiz”) was eventually hired in his place but that Dickens seized control of the project, significantly altering the ratio of text to images and turning a series of episodic sketches into a novel. With the introduction in the fourth issue of the hero’s irresistible sidekick, Sam Weller, the work really took off, and Pickwick became a best seller. The format Dickens had adopted—thirty-two-page monthly numbers with two illustrations each—became standard for Victorian fiction through the middle of the century. Seymour’s “fatal surrender,” as Dowd puts it, also marked a change in the relation between writers and illustrators, with writers now firmly in charge, while illustrators—of literary works at least—were understood as “valuable, fundamentally responsive contributors, decisively bound to an authorial text.”

That understanding of illustration probably remains the dominant one among readers of literature, even if they no longer expect to consume their fiction in monthly issues. It’s also the understanding that governs Dowd’s appealing chapter on children’s books, whose illustrations include a page from a fifteenth-century Chinese primer and a spread from Nu Dang and His Kite (1959)—a sophisticated picture book about a boy in Thailand created by the textile and fashion designer Jacqueline Ayer—as well as some prime examples from what’s been called the golden age of children’s literature: John Tenniel’s frontispiece for Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865) and a stunning two-page spread of Walter Crane’s chromolithograph for Beauty and the Beast (1875) among them.

Nothing otherwise links Tenniel’s frontispiece to Toshikata’s print of the Japanese army’s victory some three decades later, but it’s nonetheless striking how both men register their self-consciousness about art making by including figures of artists at work within their images. For Tenniel, it’s a frog slyly posed at the right-hand edge of the frame, where he’s apparently serving as the courtroom artist for the King and Queen of Hearts and the bird-headed judges arranged below.

Variations on this conceit seem to have appealed to other illustrators too. Dowd reproduces a cover created by Norman Rockwell for The Saturday Evening Post in 1961, for instance, that pictures the graphic designer Herb Lubalin at work on the magazine’s new logo, as discarded attempts dot the drawing board and old Post covers fan out behind it. Rockwell’s image of the designer at work in turn recalls a cover entitled “Blank Canvas (Deadline)” that he had produced for the same magazine more than two decades earlier, in which the artist pictured himself in the act of inventing—or rather, failing to invent—the cover in question. Yet another mischievous cover, this one by George Lois for a 1963 issue of Esquire, depicts a large billboard of Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton in Cleopatra—itself, Dowd notes, an illustration from the film’s poster—with two Lilliputian men perched on a scaffold in front of it. The men are soberly dressed, which adds to the comedy, since they also prove to be working artists, one of whom consults a reference image and draws a further line down Taylor’s cleavage.

Publications like these figure prominently in Dowd’s story. By the turn of the twentieth century the serial format popularized by Dickens had largely died out in Britain and America, and most serious writers of literature seem to have shared James’s desire to keep their pages free of other people’s images. But illustrated fiction for adults remained a significant feature of the general interest magazines that began to invade the market in the 1890s, their success buoyed by the advertisements that increasingly provided their chief source of revenue. Recent advances in photomechanical reproduction also contributed to their popularity, by enabling publishers to swap out engravings for more visually alluring halftones. Employing many of the same artists who also worked anonymously for their advertisers, magazines like McClure’s, Cosmopolitan, and their descendants in the mid-twentieth century encouraged readers to move seamlessly between both kinds of image, especially since “full-page ads,” as Dowd observes, “often included columns of copy and looked like stories.” It may be an accident that Dowd’s own eye seems to have been drawn more to the ads and magazine covers than to the pictures that accompanied the fiction inside, but his preference is also a reminder of how brief, comparatively speaking, was the era when illustrators took their marching orders from the writers of literature. Though Dowd occasionally writes as if illustration were by definition a subordinate activity—most notably, if oddly, when he refers in passing to “the practice of writers illustrating engravings with textual compositions” or adopts the same idiom for the captioning of the cartoons on the back page of The New Yorker—the majority of illustrations in Reading Pictures appear to argue otherwise.

In titling another chapter of his book “Illustrator as Author,” however, Dowd further complicates his narrative, even as he partly revises the chronology he has previously traced by beginning with Dickens. Rather than Phiz’s illustrations for Pickwick, this account opens with William Hogarth and his successful campaign to extend British copyright protection to printed multiples of visual art. The creator of A Harlot’s Progress (1732) had already turned author in Dowd’s sense by telling the tale of a young woman’s seduction and ruin through a sequence of elaborately captioned prints, themselves derived from oil paintings. But engravings like these were vulnerable to counterfeiters, and it was only with the passage of the Engraving Copyright Act of 1734 that Hogarth felt reasonably in control of his market—an achievement that constitutes a seminal moment in the history of printed images and that the artist soon celebrated by issuing another of his famous sequences, The Rake’s Progress (1735).*

Abundantly supplemented by text and filled with emblematic details that require decoding, Hogarth’s prints are clearly pictures to be read. Whether most people would identify them as illustrations is more debatable, but it is this expansive sense of the term that appears to account for many of the other examples in Dowd’s book, from newspaper cartoons and comic strips to manga and graphic novels. Or perhaps it would be more accurate to say that the title Reading Pictures is finally a better guide to Dowd’s project than his subtitle, particularly since he acknowledges at one point that “freestanding” images like cartoons or caricatures don’t really qualify, even as he continues to reproduce a number of these, together with other freestanding images, from posters to the occasional oil painting.

Though Hogarth chiefly figures here as a champion of illustrators’ intellectual property, his visual legacy is abundantly evident as well. Among the most strikingly Hogarth-like of the images in Dowd’s book is a full-page reproduction of a cartoon feature by R.F. Outcault entitled “What they did to the dog-catcher in Hogan’s Alley” that appeared in Joseph Pulitzer’s New York World in 1896 (see illustration at top of article). The cartoon’s action takes place on New York’s Lower East Side rather than in Georgian London, but its raucous urban scene still owes an obvious debt to the eighteenth-century satirist. So, too, does the sheer proliferation of detail—the flames bursting from the dogcatcher’s van, the parrot squawking in a cage suspended from the bars of a fire escape, the boy tumbling headlong into the crowd—as well as the verbal glosses that Outcault scatters, as Hogarth did before him, throughout his image. The advertisement for “McSwat’s New Gold Cure” affixed to the tenement wall is pure Hogarth, as are the lyrics of “The Park Row Songster” that lie on the ground between two dogs and spell out “Its Funny How They Roast Us When We’er Gone [sic],” especially since the dogs’ eager postures and gaping jaws make them look as if they were singing along. We might almost be looking at Hogarth’s Beer Street (1751), Gin Lane (1751), or one of The Four Stages of Cruelty (1751), though the youthful denizens of Hogan’s Alley vigorously beating the dogcatcher to keep him from turning his catch into sausage are likely to evoke far more sympathy than the children torturing dogs and other animals in the first plate of the Four Stages of Cruelty. Outcault is a less sophisticated artist than Hogarth, and his lines lack the other’s refinement, but he clearly belongs in the great printmaker’s lineage.

Dowd also highlights Outcault’s role in the evolution of the comic strip, especially after the cartoonist left Pulitzer’s paper for William Randolph Hearst’s New York Journal, where he began experimenting with telling stories in multiple panels and supplying the parrot—a favorite character, apparently—with speech bubbles. If this practice of narrating primarily through images turns the creators of comic strips and graphic novels into “author-illustrators,” in Dowd’s coinage, then the illustrations they produce are no longer the handmaidens of text but something more like its master.

One of the last examples in Reading Pictures is a page from the graphic novel It’s a Good Life, If You Don’t Weaken (1996) by the Canadian cartoonist known as Seth that virtually does away with words altogether. There’s a speech bubble in the upper left-hand panel, but apart from a street sign spelling out “Milner” at the bottom, the other five panels are wordless: a device the artist employs repeatedly in the course of the narrative, sometimes for several pages at a stretch. The effect is not quite as stark, admittedly, as that produced by one of Dowd’s earliest examples, an initial miniature from a fifteenth-century antiphony in the Siena Cathedral whose vividly painted image of Jesus healing the leper visually overwhelms the capital R of its frame.

But the graphic novel, too, plays with the possibility that “looking,” as Dowd says of the miniature, “is more important than reading,” or at least that looking can itself be a means of reading—as of course it always is. Though Dowd doesn’t explicitly register the fact, the hand lettering of a graphic novel like It’s a Good Life also hearkens back to earlier practices. The comparatively simple strokes with which Seth forms his letters may seem a long way from the fluidity and sophistication of the ideograms in the Diamond Sutra, but both the calligrapher and the cartoonist know that the writer’s mark making can also be part of the picture.

entries.title: Biden’s Choice
entries.summary: As Israel’s assault on Gaza grew worse and worse, Joe Biden and his advisers acted as though they had no option but to offer their unconditional support. Why couldn’t they see the destruction they were enabling?
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In March 2024, five months into Israel’s war on Gaza, President Joe Biden warned that an Israeli assault on the city of Rafah would cross a “red line” that would make him reconsider America’s unconditional support. At the time around 1.4 million Palestinians were huddled in Rafah, the sole crossing point for aid entering Gaza. “You cannot have 30,000 more Palestinians dead,” Biden said. But Israel went ahead with the attack, US weapons transfers continued after a sole shipment was paused, and another 30,000 Palestinians were killed in Gaza.

Near the beginning of Crossing the Red Line, his revealing book on the Biden administration’s policy in Gaza, the journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed quotes an unnamed White House official arguing that the president’s warning had in fact worked. The scale of killing in Rafah, the aide insisted, “slowed and it was not just because there was nobody left to kill.” But anyone with an Internet connection can see that Rafah was reduced to rubble. The aide’s attempt at spin reads like an indictment of the American political and national security apparatus.

The record is clear: Israel’s destruction of Gaza would not have been possible without US support. The US was Israel’s largest source of weapons, at a cost of nearly $20 billion by the end of Biden’s term. Israel dropped American-supplied bombs on civilians from American-supplied planes. To keep the weapons flowing, the Biden administration ignored legislation—including the so-called Leahy Law and Sections 502B and 620I of the Foreign Assistance Act—that restricts weapons transfers to governments suspected of committing war crimes and human rights abuses or obstructing US aid from reaching civilians.

The White House also shielded Israel from accountability. It vetoed multiple United Nations Security Council resolutions and repeatedly attacked institutions, like the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice, that challenged Israel’s conduct. The administration also discredited opposition in the US, particularly protesters on college campuses, all while dubiously casting the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as eager for a cease-fire.

By late September 2026 Israel’s US-backed bombardment had killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, 20,000 of whom were children. (The number is likely higher, with many buried under the 68 million tons of rubble in Gaza.) Many human rights organizations, a United Nations inquiry led by this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner, and dozens of leading scholars have concluded that this constitutes a genocide.

In Crossing the Red Line, Ahmed, who covered the Biden administration for HuffPost, documents how a presidency that began by promising to end wars and save democracy from authoritarianism ended in moral and political collapse. In doing so, he probes uncomfortable questions. Why did Biden choose not to exert any meaningful leverage even after it became clear that Netanyahu was ignoring his warnings? What led individual staffers to rationalize their participation in a policy that showed so little regard for human life? How did the foreign policy of a Democratic president become so untethered from any ethical or legal foundation at a time when his party was claiming to defend democratic values and the rule of law at home?

Reading Ahmed’s book, you get the sense that there was something grimly inevitable about Biden’s support for genocide; even in retrospect, officials seem incapable of believing that they could have substantially broken with Israel. But that thinking is as dangerous as it is wrong: American policy is the product of choices made by a president and his team, and we must reckon with that reality to make different choices in the future.

I went to work as a speechwriter for Barack Obama in 2007. Early in his first term, I was tasked with writing a speech, to be delivered in Cairo, that was intended to reset US relations with the Muslim world. Obama told me that his chief objective was to speak openly and honestly about issues that had become sources of tension during the George W. Bush administration.

While I was drafting the speech, senior White House staff asked me to sit down with a leader of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) who wanted to share his thoughts. One of his requests for the speech seemed innocuous: Obama should call on Muslims to recognize Israel as a Jewish state. Yet even as a thirty-one-year-old speechwriter, I understood the policy shift embedded in this request. Endorsing such a formal recognition would be taking a position on the right of return for Palestinian refugees, a so-called final status issue that was supposed to be left up to negotiations. Moreover, it would imply that non-Jewish Israelis were second-class citizens (which they effectively became in 2018 when the Knesset passed a law declaring Israel to be a state for the Jewish people).

The Cairo speech left out the call to recognize Israel as a Jewish state. Instead Obama described the US–Israel bond as “unbreakable” and denounced antisemitism and Holocaust denial. He also called the “occupation” of Palestine “intolerable” and rejected the legitimacy of Israeli settlements. “Israelis must acknowledge that just as Israel’s right to exist cannot be denied,” he said, “neither can Palestine’s.”

Advertisement

In the weeks that followed, we got pushback from members of Congress, Democratic donors, and pro-Israel media outlets and personalities. Their complaints were similar. Why hadn’t Obama traveled to Israel in addition to Egypt? Why hadn’t he referred to Israel as the historic homeland of the Jewish people? Why hadn’t he recognized Israel as a Jewish state? Over time those demands made their way into Obama’s speeches as we succumbed to the drumbeat around us.

This pattern repeated itself over eight years. For the most pro-Israel elements of the organized American Jewish community, the guiding principle has been that there should be “no daylight” between the United States and Israel. Indeed, in 2009, when Obama suggested in a meeting with community leaders that he’d have more credibility as a defender of Israel if he occasionally differed with its government, it led to attacks that persisted for years. However, the burden of ensuring US and Israeli unity was entirely on Obama: unless he aligned his public positions with those of Netanyahu, a right-winger who presided over a military occupation of Palestinian land in what I consider an apartheid system, he would pay a political price.

When Obama did break with Netanyahu—in calling for the borders of a future Palestinian state to be based on the 1967 lines with agreed-on land swaps, or in barring photographers from a meeting between the two of them—days of controversy and hyperbolic media coverage followed. Aggravated Democratic members of Congress and donors lit up the White House phone lines. Meanwhile, like clockwork, new pro-Israel legislation—providing weapons or sanctioning Iran—was introduced each year around the time of AIPAC’s policy conference in Washington and passed with overwhelming bipartisan support.

To his credit, Obama defied the wishes of an Israeli prime minister more substantially than any other president this century. Just to have the space to negotiate his nuclear deal with Iran, Obama told Democrats in the House and the Senate that he would veto their AIPAC-backed Iran sanctions bills. The result was the unprecedented sight, in 2015, of a Republican Speaker of the House inviting the prime minister of a foreign country to deliver a speech to Congress in which he lambasted American foreign policy, demanded a confrontation with Iran, and won bipartisan standing ovations for it.

When the 2015 nuclear deal was completed, pro-Israel groups spent tens of millions of dollars trying to kill it. I led a two-month effort from the Obama White House in which we relentlessly briefed and cajoled Democratic senators just to ensure we had forty votes to sustain it in the Senate. Ask yourself: Why is it so much easier to take the United States to war than to forge a diplomatic agreement to avoid one?

The enormous political capital spent in the process made it feel impossible to buck other pro-Israel priorities. After the bruising fight over the Iran deal, the Obama administration (shamefully, in retrospect) gave Netanyahu a ten-year, $38 billion memorandum of understanding for military assistance despite his intransigence on Iran and Palestine; the House of Representatives voted 405–4 to endorse it. The price of violating the no daylight rule, as with the fallout from the Cairo speech, was giving Israel other things that it wanted.

This cycle of pressure and expected accommodation inevitably shapes the behavior of the people carrying out foreign policy, who like to claim that they operate independently of politics. In private, my colleagues were often withering about Israel’s conduct. But voicing such thoughts in public was understood to be career suicide. Consider just one example. Sarah Margon, Biden’s nominee to be the State Department’s senior official responsible for democracy and human rights, was unable to achieve Senate confirmation because she once tweeted in support of Airbnb’s short-lived boycott of West Bank settlements.

Or consider me. During the Obama administration, I was known in Washington to be a critic of Israel’s policies and a pugnacious defender of the Iran deal. Yet you can find footage of me online reiterating Israel’s right to defend itself in Gaza, trumpeting the unprecedented security assistance that we provided, and reciting talking points about a two-state solution while the Israeli government was making that an impossibility. At the time it felt anodyne; in retrospect it doesn’t.

Still, by the end of the Obama administration, the pro-Israel media was attacking me relentlessly and prominent donors were occasionally chewing me out. In 2018 I learned through press reports that a group of former Mossad agents known as Black Cube was digging up dirt on me. Operatives had even contacted my wife under the false pretense of being a movie production company: the aptly named “Shell Productions.” None of this was subtle. Indeed it was so heavy handed that it almost seemed as if Black Cube wanted these efforts to become public. Perhaps that was the point of the vitriol directed at me: to show other people working in US national security what they could expect if they strayed from the no daylight approach.
